t.E127.agn: On 15 January 2025 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) revoked its authorisation in food because of a tumour finding at high doses in male rats; in the same statement it said there was no evidence showing harm in humans. In the EU it is authorised only in a limited range of products.
t.E127.body: In rats, orally ingested erythrosine is largely excreted unchanged in faeces; no dye was found in urine. Erythrosine is stable in the body and is excreted without releasing its iodine. When 16 mg a day was given to humans for 10 days, the level of protein-bound iodine in the blood rose temporarily and returned to its previous level within three months.
t.E127.eff.0.a: High dose in an animal study
t.E127.eff.0.t: Because tumours were seen at high doses in male rats, its authorisation in food was revoked in the US in 2025; the FDA stated that there was no evidence showing harm in humans
t.E127.eval: The US FDA revoked its authorisation on 15 January 2025 because of a tumour finding in male rats (final date for use in food: 15 January 2027); the FDA also states that there is no evidence of harm in humans. In the EU it is authorised only in a limited range of products such as cocktail and candied cherries.
t.E127.prod: Produced by chemical synthesis through the iodination of fluorescein.
t.E127.summary: A synthetic, pinkish-red dye. It has been used in cocktail cherries and some confectionery.
t.agency.FDA_revoked_2025: Its authorisation in food and ingested drugs was revoked.
